Motivation The core Dynamic Containers feature ([product spec]( adds on change + .open for lazy execution and programmatic control via session state. However, some use cases benefit from updating container state imperatively within the same script run — e.g., auto-expanding an expander after data loads, switching to a results tab after computation, or auto-closing a popover after form submission. st.status already supports this pattern via .update(). Extending it to expander, tabs, and popover would be a natural and consistent addition. Workaround Most .update() use cases can already be achieved using session state + on change callbacks once the core Dynamic Containers feature lands. For example, instead of exp.update(open=True), you can set st.session state.my expander = True via a button callback and let the rerun reflect the new state: The .update() method would improve on this by allowing state changes within the same script run without an explicit st.rerun() call — matching the ergonomics of st.status.update(). Proposed API st.expander — auto-expand after loading st.tabs — switch to results tab Note: st.tabs currently returns a Sequence[DeltaGenerator], so .update() would be called on individual tab objects. A tabs.update(active="Results") API would require changing the return type while preserving sequence unpacking — a design consideration for implementation. st.popover — auto-close after form submission Design Notes - The .update() method uses open as a unified parameter name across all three elements, consistent with the .open property introduced in the core feature. This was chosen over element-specific names (expanded, default, etc.) for cross-element consistency — see the product spec's "Alternative naming" discussion. - This builds on the core Dynamic Containers feature (lazy execution via on change + .open) and should be implemented after that lands. Related Issues - 6004 — Dynamic tabs (230+ upvotes) — core feature that this extends - 8265 — Add open/close parameter to st.popover — .update(open=False) addresses the programmatic close use case - 2399 — st.expander expanded/collapsed state (93+ upvotes) References - [Product spec — Dynamic Tabs, Expander, and Popover]( - [Prototype PR 13277](

Enhancement: Rerun-resilient streaming (st.write stream that survives widget interactions) Problem st.write stream blocks the script thread while iterating through a generator. If a user interacts with any widget while streaming is in progress, Streamlit's rerun model kills the current script run — and the stream along with it. For LLM chat apps, this means typing a follow-up message or clicking any button while a response is streaming causes the in-progress response to be lost mid-output. This is one of the most common pain points for LLM-powered apps built with Streamlit. The workaround today is to disable all interactive widgets while streaming, which is a poor user experience. How st.write stream works today st.write stream iterates synchronously through a generator on the script thread. It normalizes OpenAI/LangChain chunks to strings, renders them progressively via an st.empty() placeholder with markdown(unterminated parsing=True), and returns the full accumulated response when the generator is exhausted. The entire iteration blocks the script thread. Because the script thread is blocked, the yield point mechanism (which checks for pending rerun requests at st. calls) fires inside the markdown update on each chunk. If a rerun is pending, the script run is interrupted, the generator is abandoned, and partial output is lost. Proposed solution A mode for streaming that moves the iteration off the script thread so the stream continues across reruns. The stream's output container is preserved (not garbage-collected by clearStaleNodes) and continues receiving chunks even as the main script re-executes. Option A — parameter on existing API: Option B — separate API: In both cases, the call returns immediately with a handle/placeholder rather than blocking until the stream completes. The stream runs in a managed thread with ScriptRunContext access (it needs to call st. internally to render chunks). On subsequent reruns, the script re-encounters the call and either attaches to the in-progress stream or renders the completed result. Design considerations - Return type change: st.write stream currently returns the full response synchronously (str | list[Any]). A background version returns immediately — different semantics. This favors Option B (separate API) to avoid confusion. - Container preservation: The streaming container must survive clearStaleNodes during reruns, similar to how run every fragments preserve their containers. - Thread with ScriptRunContext: Unlike background tasks (see "What this is NOT" below), the streaming thread does need ScriptRunContext because it calls st. markdown internally to render chunks. This is a key architectural difference. - Cancellation semantics: When should a background stream stop? Options include: session close, explicit cancel, or starting a new stream with the same key. - Fragment infrastructure reuse: The fragment system already handles container preservation across reruns and thread management. Background streaming could build on this infrastructure. What this is NOT This proposal is not the same as background tasks / background execution ([ 6687]( The distinction: | | Background tasks | Rerun-resilient streaming | |---|---|---| | Renders UI? | No — produces data, no st. calls | Yes — renders progressively (token by token) | | Needs ScriptRunContext? | No | Yes — calls st. internally | | Core concern | Move long computation outside the script run | Keep UI output flowing across reruns | | Return value | Data result (accessed on next rerun) | Rendered content in the app | Background tasks are about computation that doesn't touch the UI. Rerun-resilient streaming is about UI rendering that shouldn't be interrupted. They are complementary ideas that address different problems. Related issues - 10578 — "Input events immediately terminate everything." The core motivation: widget interactions kill in-progress work including streaming. - 6687 — Background execution (16 👍). Related but distinct — covers headless computation, not UI streaming. Additional context Within a parallel fragment (@st.fragment(parallel=True), under development), st.write stream would already run on a worker thread and not block the main script. However, parallel fragments don't solve the cross-rerun problem — the join barrier at scriptFinished cancels worker threads, so the stream still doesn't survive a rerun triggered by widget interaction. This proposal specifically addresses the cross-rerun resilience gap.

st.yield point — cooperative cancellation checkpoint for long-running code Problem Streamlit's execution model uses yield points to interrupt a running script when a rerun is pending (e.g. a user clicked a widget). These yield points fire automatically inside most st. calls — whenever the script enqueues a ForwardMsg, the runtime checks for pending reruns and raises RerunException if one is waiting. This works well for typical apps, but breaks down when user code spends significant time in a tight loop or a blocking call without calling any st. command. In that case, the script runner can't interrupt the code until the blocking call returns — the rerun is queued but not observed. The app feels frozen: This is an existing limitation today with sequential scripts, but it becomes more visible with parallel fragments (planned): a dashboard with 10 parallel fragments each doing a 30-second query means a widget click waits up to 30 seconds for the slowest thread to reach a yield point. Current workarounds Users can insert a dummy st.empty() call to create an implicit yield point, but this is: - Non-obvious — requires understanding Streamlit's internal execution model - Semantically wrong — st.empty() creates a UI element, not a cancellation checkpoint - Fragile — relies on an implementation detail (that element emission checks for pending reruns) Proposed API A no-op in terms of UI — it doesn't render anything or modify state. It simply checks whether a rerun is pending and, if so, cooperatively stops the current execution so the rerun can proceed. Usage Behavior - Main script thread: Checks ScriptRequests.on scriptrunner yield(). If a full rerun is pending, raises RerunException. If only fragment-scoped reruns are pending, returns immediately (no preemption). - Sequential fragments: Same as main thread — checks for pending reruns. - Parallel fragment threads: Checks for pending reruns that would cancel the current fragment execution (full-app reruns, thread cancellation signals). - No pending rerun: Returns immediately with negligible overhead (one lock acquisition on ScriptRequests). - Outside Streamlit context: No-op (graceful degradation, same pattern as other st. commands that check for ScriptRunContext). Why a new command (not a parameter on an existing one) st.yield point() serves a fundamentally different purpose from existing commands — it's about execution control, not rendering or state. It belongs in the same family as st.rerun() and st.stop(): imperative control flow commands. Adding it as a parameter on an existing element (e.g. st.empty(yield point=True)) would overload a rendering command with execution control semantics. Relationship to other features - Parallel fragments (@st.fragment(parallel=True)): st.yield point() is independently useful, but becomes especially valuable with parallel fragments where multiple threads may be doing long-running work. It gives users a way to make their parallel fragment code responsive to cancellation. Related issues - 2838 — "Trigger a script re-run from another thread" (30 reactions). That issue asks for st.request rerun() to signal a rerun from outside the script thread. st.yield point() is the complementary direction — checking for pending interrupts within a thread. Together they'd give users full cooperative concurrency control.

Layout containers (tabs, expander, popover) should persist frontend state automatically without requiring key= Summary st.tabs, st.expander, and st.popover lose their frontend state (selected tab, open/closed) when the component remounts due to structural changes in the render tree — for example, when a conditional element above the container is toggled between reruns. As of [ 14330]( [ 14332]( and [ 14356]( this is solved for containers that have an explicit key= parameter . When a user provides key=, the container's identity is stabilized and its frontend state persists across remounts. However, containers without an explicit key= still lose state on remount. Ideally, state persistence would work automatically without requiring the user to understand delta path shifts or know to add a key. Current Behavior Workaround (available today) Adding key= to the affected container stabilizes its identity and persists state: Desired Behavior Containers should maintain their frontend state across reruns automatically, even without key=, when structural changes above them cause a remount. Context This is a follow-up to [ 8239]( (89 upvotes), which tracked the original state-loss problem. That issue is now closed as the key-based persistence solution has shipped. This issue tracks the remaining case: automatic persistence without requiring an explicit key. Approaches under consideration are documented in an internal investigation spec covering per-type call counters, code-position capture, structural hashing, and hybrid strategies. Each has trade-offs around stability when same-type elements are conditionally rendered.

Add block-no-verify hooks to prevent agents from bypassing git hooks Feature: Add block-no-verify hooks to prevent agents from bypassing git hooks Streamlit's .claude/settings.json and .cursor/hooks.json already have excellent quality enforcement (pre-commit, autofix, tests). There's one gap: the git hook-bypass flag. When an agent runs git commit or git push with the hook-bypass flag, it silently skips pre-commit hooks, commit-msg validation, and pre-push test suites — the very checks configured in Streamlit's hooks system. Proposed fix Add block-no-verify@1.1.2 ([github.com/tupe12334/block-no-verify]( to both agent configs: Claude Code — add a Bash PreToolUse hook before the existing pre bash redirect.py: Cursor — add a command beforeShellExecution hook before the existing prompt hooks: The package reads the command from the hook stdin, detects the hook-bypass flag across all git subcommands, and exits 2 to block. All existing hooks are preserved unchanged. --- Disclosure: I am the author and maintainer of block-no-verify.

Enable key as main identity=True for stateful layout containers Summary PR 14330 introduced stable Block.id for st.tabs, st.expander, and st.popover using compute and register element id with key as main identity=False. This means the element ID incorporates all parameters (label, tab count, etc.) alongside the user key. The next step is to test and enable key as main identity=True so that the identity is based solely on the user-provided key. This would allow dynamic changes to container parameters (tab labels, tab count, expander label) without invalidating the stored frontend state — the container would retain its Block.id as long as the key stays the same. Why not now key as main identity=True requires careful testing to ensure that dynamic parameter changes (e.g., adding/removing tabs, renaming labels) are handled correctly without breaking the container state or producing visual glitches. This was deferred from 14330 to keep the initial change focused and low-risk. Scope - Test key as main identity=True for st.tabs, st.expander, and st.popover - Verify dynamic parameter changes (label renames, tab additions/removals) work correctly - Ensure elementStates entries are cleaned up properly - Update the tech spec at specs/2026-02-26-layout-container-state-persistence/tech-spec.md References - 14330 — Stable Block.id for passive keyed layout containers - 8239 — Original user request for state persistence

Add a dropdown selector to st.chat input similar to LLM chat interfaces Checklist - [x] I have searched the [existing issues]( for similar feature requests. - [x] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue. Summary Add a dropdown selector to st.chat input, similar to the pattern used in ChatGPT and other LLM chat interfaces. This could either: - extend the current accept file=True behavior, or - be introduced as a separate selector component attached to st.chat input Right now, this kind of UI is not really possible to implement cleanly without something like st.bottom. Why? For data analysis workflows, it is often important to specify exactly which dataset, table, or context the model should use. A selector attached to st.chat input would make that context explicit before submission, which helps: - reduce ambiguity about which data the model should query - avoid hallucinated joins or incorrect assumptions across tables - support more targeted system prompts - make it easier to drive different output modes, such as plain text, charts, or HTML reports. Example use case A user might choose one of the following before sending a message: - a specific table - a semantic layer or query target - an output mode such as text, chart, or report That gives the app a structured way to route the prompt and configure the model behavior before the message is processed.
